utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Let us have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours please, my name is Grant Niemann, I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with Mr. Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, along with my colleague Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am John Ackerman. Cynthia McMurrey and I are appearing here today on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have a witness available today. Before I move on to that witness, in relation to matters raised yesterday, firstly, in terms of the issue of what the Prosecution's obligation is concerning discovery of articles and so forth of an expert witness, I have obtained a copy of the relevant decision of the Trial Chamber in the Blaskic case, the decision of 27th January 1997. It is instructive in paragraph 40, which I have highlighted, as to the obligations, namely that there are none on the Prosecution to produce this material. I make available that copy to the Defence and to your Honours. I shall do that. In addition, your Honours, I have extracted my personal copy of the Gow articles, which I reluctantly make available to the Defence. I say reluctantly because they have my markings on and my own work product. I think it is to me unreasonable that I should have to make available material which has my own workings and markings on it. In the interest of trying to get this matter done I have four copies. I do not vouch for the fact they cover everything that Dr. Gow has ever written. I know the fact -- I know for a fact that he has written other material. I do not consider it in any way my responsibility to do their research. If they wish to research other matters it is up to them to do so. No responsibility falls on the Prosecution's shoulders in that regard. In addition to that your Honours, I am going to -- Dr. Gow is coming to The Hague over the weekend. I am not going to stop him from doing that. I think he should still come to The Hague, but in the event that the Defence are not in a position to cross-examine him at the conclusion of his evidence-in-chief it is my application to your Honours that I do not call him, that we arrange for another witness to be made available. There is also the issue of the outstanding argument on the admissibility of the Austrian documents which I think will probably take some time. We can utilise, I think, our time very usefully in that way. But if the Defence are not ready I would be asking your Honours that I do not have to call him to take his evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me respond in two ways. First of all, I am grateful to Mr. Niemann for clarifying the issue of the Prosecution's responsibility in this regard, and it is now very clear when looking at what he supplied us this morning what that is. With that in mind, I have not even looked at the documents that Mr. Niemann supplied us this morning. If he truly feels by supplying those he is divulging information that he should not be divulging to us in terms of the notes he has on them, I will be pleased to hand my copy back, because that is totally in his province whether he might disclose any notes or markings he might have made on these documents. I feel very uncomfortable being in possession of those unless he absolutely agrees he has no problem with that whatsoever. Finally, with regard to his last submission that he should not call Dr. Gow next week but perhaps put him off to the time when there is no possibility of the problem we discussed yesterday existing, I can only say this to the Trial Chamber: having not looked at the documents Mr. Niemann has supplied I do not know whether or not all the documents from Jayne's are contained in there or not. We did not receive the documents from Jayne's yesterday. There is that period of time until 5 o'clock today when they could be received. If they are received there will not be any problem; if they are not, then there will be and I think I would be entitled to make the same kind of application we made yesterday with regard to Mr. Economides. I can only say we have been diligent and in good faith trying to gather these documents together. Probably in the interest of fairness and efficiency Mr. Niemann's request that Mr. Gow be put off until our December sitting or whenever he had in mind might very well avoid a problem next week. I leave it up to the Trial Chamber, but that is the best I can do right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Along the same lines; first I would like to thank Mr. Niemann for providing this. I placed mine upside down. If there is any way he can extract, cover up, black out, white out, whatever, any of his notes, I frankly would feel more comfortable with these. As for a scheduling, if he would be more comfortable putting Dr. Gow off that is fine with us. If he is more comfortable putting other witnesses on, I noticed there were like six names on the list, four names he just gave us on a list for next week, to save Professor Gow a trip, if that is what Mr. Niemann thinks would be appropriate or necessary. Whatever makes his scheduling easier, because we understand the problems and we know we will be facing the same problems of international plane travel and scheduling witnesses and things like that. I am willing to go along with whatever Mr. Niemann thinks might make it easier for him to present his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am indebted to my colleagues for that. Your Honours, with respect to the material itself there are only markings on the material, I have taken the precaution of removing my hand-written notes. Nevertheless, that does indicate the areas of the articles I concentrated on. I do not mind if that material is seen by Defence counsel; if they feel they may benefit from my notes, so be it. If the Defence feel it may be helpful to them, then my markings are there for them to look at. I think it would be proper that Dr. Gow does not testify on Monday and Tuesday as was planned. I think that obviously, from what has been said now, the Defence are not in a position at the moment and it is likely they will not be in a position on Monday. For that reason I think if we can we will try to make other arrangements. If I have any further news on that aspect of the matter during the course of today I will inform the Chamber about that. If your Honours please -- excuse me. I might just foreshadow your Honour, we will put in a written motion but we do intend -- your Honours have not seen the list of witnesses for next week, but one of the witnesses that we do intend to call during the course of next week is a United Nations security officer. We will need to seek your Honour's leave to call that witness and we will file a motion in that respect during the course of today. In addition, your Honours, we will be, in the course of next week, endeavouring to recall a witness that was called previously, with the pseudonym Witness J. I do not believe I need leave to file an application for leave for that. If your Honours would prefer I can incorporate that in the motion as well. So I just foreshadow that it may transpire that we -- those witnesses may be moved forward and give their evidence early in the course of next week. It was proposed that they would give their evidence in the latter part of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When you might have seen your position let me know what the arrangements can be. Let us have your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Adem Omerkic. (Witness enters court) ADEM OMERKIC, (sworn) Examination-in-chief by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name, your Honours, my name is Adem Omerkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Omerkic, did you complete studies at the University of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your field of study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I studied at the faculty of philosophy, comparative literature and library work, and I graduated at that department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do post-graduate studies in political science?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am now attending post-graduate courses at the faculty of political sciences in Sarajevo. I have another examination left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially on the 8th April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you take part in the military activities in and around Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I participated in the defence, the defence of Sarajevo, in the defence against aggression. We were attacked. We were defending ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Captain by rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position do you hold at the moment in the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am acting head of the department for archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you become acting head of the department for archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially on the 1st March I assumed that duty when my predecessor retired; and in the second of 1996, no 1997 -- I am a bit confused. I was appointed for as acting, acting head of the department for archive materials, but on March 1st this year I actually assumed that office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you first become involved in working with the archives of the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation? When did you first become involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the first time that was in the second half of 1996 or 1997 -- I am sorry, I just do not know. I am confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do not be too nervous, try to settle down. Just relax a bit. Can you tell the court what the purpose of this archive is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of the archives is to gather documentation from the period of aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the military documentation, to collect, process and prepare those documents so that they can be properly filed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The documents that you archive, are they exclusively military documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly, yes; but sometimes there are documents that somehow get their way there and there are also some documents from the former Ministry of Defence, from before the war. But that is of a lesser quantity. Mainly we collect documents during the aggression, that is documents from the units who were there. This mainly has to do with orders, reports, operative log books and that sort of thing, analysis --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, I interrupted you. Keep going. The documents that you collect, are they documents from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or does the collection include other documents such as captured documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that mostly these are documents from our units; but there is a smaller proportion of captured documents, captured materials, but this is a smaller, insignificant part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the acting chief of the document archives, what are your duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My duty is to work on the filing and processing and actually the implementation of the provisional rules sent to all our units. That is, we are engaged in an effort to establish a system of keeping records in our units, so that to keep them in a more systematic way, so that we have sent certain rules, and some of my staff have toured units on the ground to try to help them implement this. Therefore, my duty is to organise the work and to control the work and to do everything that needs to be done to organise the archives, though this is not really the archives as a whole, but it is a department of the archives dealing with documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you strive to make sure that your documents are maintained in a proper order and good condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I do. We had many problems, and we had problems throughout the aggression. There was a shortage of paper and other essentials, and there was also a fire in the building where the archives were kept. I personally participated in the efforts to put out the fire and a chandelier fell on my head so I actually personally participated in saving the documentation from that building and we worked on it until late at night. That is one of the ways, though we do not have adequate conditions even now, but we are striving to protect what we have, to make a system out of it, and we are also working on continued collecting of material. So we are doing our best. I personally am trying -- am doing my best, and so are members of my staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members of staff do you have working for you, Mr. Omerkic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I and four women, four members of staff -- five, actually, including myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you mentioned earlier that you have set procedures, do you, for the collection and maintenance and processing of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that we have provisional rules, provisional regulations, which are not treated as anything permanent. These are provisional regulations, covering a definite period, the period of aggression. In view of the specific nature of the material from that period, these regulations have been adopted as provisional ones and as such have been sent to all units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the past and today was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina divided into different corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There is the general staff, then there were five corps, then there were the brigades, smaller units and then still smaller units were companies, and so on. So yes, the armed forces were divided into corps, four corps and each corps had to have a person responsible for, in the administration, responsible for the archives, and in smaller units that depended on needs and possibilities. Everybody was supposed to work in that area, but there were problems there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the archives of the actual corps themselves, where are they located? Are they located with the corps or are they located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An order regulated and determined a date by when all the documentation had to be submitted to the central archives, but this deadline was postponed. Because of the situation linked with the fire we had to extend the deadline, and since we are working under impossible conditions, but we are still working, we have postponed this deadline so that the people in the corps should continue working on those documents and preparing them for hand-over, but that they should keep them in the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that you have some documents in your collection but some documents are still in the archive of the corps, but you anticipate that ultimately they will all come over to your archive. Is that a summary of the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and we hope that that will happen, or rather those are the orders given to those units, and the people working there have an obligation to hand them over; but then there too there are problems, because the continuous transformations made in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina have resulted in many people being demobilised and in the archives people were usually working who were, as a result of the transformation, demobilised, so this problem was not quite adequately addressed, sufficient attention was not devoted to these activities so that we are having problems with the collecting of these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some of the documents were lost and others presumably destroyed. I gather others may have been taken by people leaving the army or following demobilisation, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible. There may have been such cases, though I do not know. But I know that there were cases that we would find a whole pile of documents, sometimes the documents would be placed in inadequate conditions, so it may have been humid or something. So there may have been individuals who took some documents with them, but there are documents that we are still searching for and that is part of our work too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, your collection is not a complete collection and nor would you presumably expect it to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not complete and we do not expect that we will ever be able to collect everything; but we are trying very hard; in view of the very difficult conditions under which we are working, we are doing our best to collect as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What arrangements are in place for documents to be delivered to your archive from the various sources from which you receive it? Do you have any set procedures in place for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the usual manner of our work. We cannot go after an individual and ask him about documents if he is no longer there, for instance a commander of a unit, if he has left or he had died, we do not know what happened to his documents; but wherever we have a possibility through the official military channels, through our own orders, where we are able to direct people to work towards turning it over to us, this is what we are working on, wherever we have a possibility. Where we do not ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How are the documents physically maintained in your archive? How do you keep them in the archive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that because of the fire that we had the building is no longer fit, so we had to put everything in the park and then into another building and then into a third building and practically we just piled up all these registers on top of one another because we did not have any shelving and we did not have any other space where to put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you a bit? I was perhaps a little misleading. How do you organise the documents in the archive, not physically how they are stacked or kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. We have divided them by corps, so by the unit, and within each register there are -- the reports are separate, orders are separate, operations, log books are separate. So it is by the subject. It is classified by the subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there a, in your collection, a binder or a collection specified for the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We have not one binder but several binders, maybe one binder was particularly relevant here, but there is a lot of documents -- there are a lot of documents. So the 4th Corps, for the units of the 4th Corps there are quite a few documents. However, with the transformation, with the 3rd and 4th Corps they are practically dissolved, so all the documents from the 3rd and the 4th Corps have been inherited by the unit that is now in existence there, which is a division. So they have now the obligation to take care of these documents so that these documents can be turned over to us. So it is not one binder, there are multiple binders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you first receive documents -- when did you first receive documents from the 4th Corps into your archive? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I first arrived the documents of the 3rd and 4th Corps were in the process of being turned over. The archive of the 4th Corps was being delivered, but it was not processed professionally, so it was returned to them in order to get processed. When I arrived these materials have been processed properly, and together with the other staff I was there when it was delivered to us. So that was my first contact with the documents of the 4th Corp. And later I also took part, this was later after four or five months, when they gather further documents from their units or they deliver it to us and we take it over and if we -- we looked it over and if certain things were not properly processed we would return them to them so -- in order for it to be properly processed. So this is an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did examine the documents that you received from the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a part of it, part of the documents. I had -- I reviewed part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know a General in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the name Delic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my client appreciates the promotion and wonders whether the salary will come with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the joint army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina is General Rasim Delic, and you have had something else in mind maybe, it is not clear to me, but this is the Commander Delic and the person who --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he give you an order to locate certain documents in your archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the normal practice, that I received an order by the General that I should provide certain documents for somebody's review; but this is the proper way for me to get from General Delic an order, he issues a document for me to turn it over to someone else to look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When General Delic gives you an order in relation to handing over documents, what steps do you take in order to keep a record of the documents that you issue to third parties? What do you do when you do this, when you comply with your order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, this is an usual practice. Whichever document we issue to another party, we register it and we keep this record, and we compile a report to our superiors. So we keep a ledger of the documents that were issued to other parties that we keep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September of 1997, this year, did you receive an order from General Delic concerning the making available of certain documents to this Tribunal, the International Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do when you received that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with my staff we immediately embarked on the task. We formed a task force so that we could deliver all the documents in our possession, and we did as much as we could, given, again, the difficult circumstances under which we work. So we were all involved in looking for these documents and for providing the photocopies of these documents. Parallel to that, I had other obligations in the 3rd Corps, so part of the staff work there, so we had this task force that were responsible directly to the General for this task, and the part of the team went to the 3rd Corps and this 3rd Corps was also dissolved last month. So we went down there in order to receive the documents that they still had in their possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will not ask you about the 3rd Corps, I think. I think we will just keep to the 4th Corp. Now, with the documents that you extracted, did you keep a record of these documents and did you review the documents that you had extracted from the archives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we register them, and recorded them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the documents that you extracted, did you make a list for your own personal records of the ones that you had extracted from the archives and had made available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We did. We made a list and we kept it in this ledger, so that we know what we issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What matters -- what aspects of a document do you rely on when you are in the process of authenticating the document for your archive? What physical characteristics of the document do you look for in order to satisfy yourself that the document is a genuine document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, it is the stamps. The stamps for which we know how they look, what colour they are, so visually they are immediately recognisable. Also certain signatures, which by now we have remembered quite well, and also the look of certain documents, the format. The manner of correspondence we can recognise, but the stamps are the key factor for recognition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now in addition to that, when you enter a document into the archive and satisfy yourself as to its authenticity, do members of the staff of the archive, including yourself, make any markings on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we process the documents myself and my staff all -- not only us in the, in the central archives, but also in the units, we classify things, because when we first get the documents they are all mixed together. So when processing we take a lead pencil and up at the top we just write down the register number, so with just lead pencil we write down 1, 2, 3, so that we would make our work easier for ourselves; but this -- because it is lead pencil this can be just erased very easily, so this is what we have resorted to, but that is sort of the leeway that we have given ourselves. So just with a lead pencil up at the top. It was just to facilitate our own, and simplify our own work. And also too when we look for a document, and let us say we have a list of documents there and we have under item 10 from such and such a date, so that we would not look for all the data, we just look for this number written in this lead pencil and that makes it easier for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are the documents that you keep in your archive relied on by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation as genuine records for the purposes of the operation and business of that army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule, the originals cannot be taken out of the archives, but on General's orders we provide a copy. So if the person is -- if a party is interested we are giving them a copy but because of the General's order the originals never leave the archive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think maybe you did not fully understand my question. I will re-phrase it if I can. The documents that are kept in your archive, are they used from time to time by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the genuine records of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Authentic, yes, yes. But again with the General's order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you are saying is not the originals but copies are used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now would you look at the document that I now show you. If your Honours please, it is now admitted as an exhibit, Defence Exhibit D120/1. But I will show the witness the copy I have here, and there is a copy for the Defence as well. There is also a copy for your Honours. It may be easier. Could I just check that there is not confusion? I want to make sure that we have the right one. Perhaps this one is a very poor copy. That is your copy there. Would you give the witness the better copy, the copy that is clearer, so attach it to that one and give it to the witness; and these ones here are the English version of it. What has happened, I just explain it now, what is going on. These documents were copied for the benefit of the Defence, and they had copies given to them some weeks ago. Madam Residovic tendered this particular document during the course of the cross-examination of I think it was General Divjak. The copy, because it is a photocopy of a photocopy of a photocopy, the quality of them has been disintegrating. The copy I am asking the witness to look at is the best original copy we had. If you could see that it would help, because there are markings on this document which he can see which no longer appear on the original exhibit. If I may I will ask that the copy of the version that the witness looks at be attached to the exhibit, if that is in order. He has not been given the copy, after all that. Would you please give him a copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is this Tactical Group 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is a reference up the top there to Tactical Group 2. I see that, your Honour. Perhaps just looking at the one that you have now been shown, Mr. Omerkic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you permit me, sir, may I refer to my notes, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you ask their Honours' permission to look at your notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You may refer to your notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am seeking permission from the court to consult my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is a better translation of the one which was provided by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it makes more sense.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, this is the -- there is an original of this document in my archive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you recognise this document as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me this is a document first of all that was signed by the then chief of the army, and was stamped with the proper stamp. My assumption is that it is in red colour, the stamp, and very clearly stamped. I remember that we searched for this one quite a long time, but it is there in our archive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a document that is relied on as a genuine document of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We consider it authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That has been tendered, so I will not seek to tender it, your Honours. Perhaps that document may now be handed back to the Registrar. The next document, if your Honours please, has been tendered as an exhibit. It is Exhibit 132/1. Again, might these documents with the original exhibit and the copy that I have provided be married together, because again the photocopy is a slightly better copy and the translation is slightly different as well. Might a copy be provided to the Defence and their Honours? Might the witness be shown a copy of the exhibit that I have provided? Again, Mr. Omerkic, by looking at that document do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document whose original exists in my archive, and it is signed by the chief of the army, a document that I know quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by reference to the markings that you see on that document, are you able to say whether you consider it to be a genuine record of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can. It is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not tender that, your Honours, because again it has been tendered previously. Mr. Omerkic, could the documents in front of you be returned to Madam Registrar? Would you look at the documents that you are shown? This document has not as yet been introduced. It will need to be allocated the next number in order for the Prosecution exhibits. Might the copies be given to the Defence and to their Honours, and a copy of the Serbo-Croat version handed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor Exhibit 195.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Omerkic, would you please look at the document that you are now shown? A copy of this document has previously been provided to Defence counsel. Mr. Omerkic, do you recognise that document that you have there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually this is a copy of the original which we have in our archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having regard to the markings that you see upon that document, do you consider it to be a genuine document of the army of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we do consider it to be an authentic document of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, it is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that document be now returned to Madam Registrar? This is again a document that has not, as yet, been tendered. A copy has previously been provided to the Defence. Might the witness be shown the version of the document in Serbo-Croat? Might the two versions of the document be handed to the Defence and to their Honours. Might it be given the number next in order for the Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor document 196.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Omerkic, do you recognise the document that you now have before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document, but here I do not see clearly the stamp. The stamp can hardly be seen, but I think that in the original there is a stamp and I have noted it down. Therefore we do have the original. But on the copy the stamp is not visible. But I do consider it to be authentic and quite true to the original which we have in our archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see on the document any markings that have been made by your archive which would indicate to you in addition whether or not it is an authentic document of the archive? Can you tell us what it is that you would look to for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see our numbers that we put down, 69, we can see that I think it is. This was written by us with an ordinary pencil, so I recognise by that in addition to everything else when I was telling you about the ordinal numbers we would put on a document. So this was one of our staff who put down this number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number 69 appears towards the top of the page, slightly to the right of the centre of the page. It is faint but it can be seen, 69?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is written in an ordinary pencil, so one of our staff wrote that down when processing the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Exhibit 196 Prosecution's is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that exhibit be removed from in front of the witness? Could the witness be shown the Serbo-Croat version of this document? There are copies for the Defence and for their Honours. This is a document that has not previously been introduced, so it needs to be allocated the next number in order for Prosecution exhibits. It is a copy -- a copy of the document has been made available previously to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor Exhibit 197.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you would like to wait a moment, Mr. Omerkic, because we have to make sure everyone gets a copy first before we talk about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Omerkic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a document that we have in our archives. It is quite recognisable by all its elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having regard to the markings that you see on the document, do you consider it to be a genuine document of the archive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, by the markings and everything else, yes, it does exist in our archives. We have the original of this copy, photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document if your Honour pleases. Might that exhibit be removed from the front of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 197 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now might this document be shown to the witness, the original version in Serbo-Croat. There are copies available for the Defence and for your Honours. The document was previously provided to the Defence. This is a new document. It has not been introduced previously, so it will need to be allocated the next number in order of the Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor Exhibit 198.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Omerkic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the markings that appear upon the document, do you recognise it as a genuine document of your archive, being a genuine document of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. I recognise it, and as such it exists, the original exists in our archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that document, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Exhibit 198 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that document be removed from the front of the witness? Might the Serbo-Croat version of this document be handed to the witness while copies of it be made available to the Defence and their Honours. This is a document that has previously been provided to the Defence. It is a document that has not as yet been previously introduced into these proceedings, so it will need to be allocated the next number in order of the Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I address the court?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, everyone needs to get a copy first before we talk about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor Exhibit 199.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Omerkic, firstly you wanted to say something. What you would like to say about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to say with regard to all these documents I hear the expression being used "Serbo-Croatian version". We in Bosnia have adopted the possibility of documents being written in Serbian Croatian but also Bosnian. Therefore all these documents were written in the Bosnian version. That is just a remark I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do apologise, I will refer to it as Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: National feelings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I did not mean any offence by that. Mr. Omerkic, just looking at the document that I have now shown to you, do you recognise that document as an authentic document of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that document be removed from in front of the witness? Might this document be married with exhibit which has previously been entered, D81/1. It is a slightly perhaps -- the translation is our translation, so it may be slightly different. In addition to that it may be a better copy of the original. If that could be placed with Exhibit D81/1. Might the Bosnian version of the copy that I have provided be given to the witness? Just while that is happening, your Honours, I have been advised that apparently when your Honour admitted Exhibit 199 into evidence it is not recorded on the transcript. It does not appear on the transcript. I heard your Honour say it was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just note that. Let us get something clear from the witness; is there any material difference between Bosnian and Serbo-Croatian so that I might know the differences in the translation, because there might be differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will ask the witness if he can tell us. He is an educated man, he may know. Mr. Omerkic, are you able to answer his Honour's question about the difference between the Serbian language and the Croatian language and the Bosnian language? Can you assist his Honour with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We in Bosnia always considered it to be one language, but since the aggressor side have made two variants, the Serbian and Croatian, in the defence for our homeland we fought for our own version. In my opinion they are absolutely the same and the differences are quite minor in the sense of the meaning of these documents. There are no differences. It is one language, in my opinion, but there may be some dialects. Basically it is all the same, but let us call it Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are trying to avoid a situation where one translation might be criticised as different.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, to clarify the previous question, the document of the 24th of November 1992, marked as 5199, the Prosecutor has suggested that it is put together with one of the Defence exhibits, that is with Defence Exhibit 81/1. So if I have misunderstood that I want to be sure, because otherwise according to my records, these are not the same documents. So I should like clarification to be made of that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I may be moving a little quickly, your Honour. The last document we dealt with was Exhibit 199. That was a Prosecution exhibit, I tendered that as a Prosecution exhibit. The document I have now just shown to the witness is a copy of document D81/1. Perhaps Madam Registrar can just check that they are the same. I think there may be some confusion. It was the previous document 199 that was already tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document of 24th November is 199.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The document D81/1, and the one I have just made available for identification by the witness is a document dated 14th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is the document of the 14th August 1992 that I am asking to be married with Exhibit D81/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 81/1, your Honour. I do not know whether that is clarified it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid it is still not quite clear to me. Could the Registry please confirm whether those are identical documents under this number of Defence exhibits, because I may have put the wrong number down, but we must make sure whether these are identical documents in Serbo-Croatian Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually the proper method is not for Prosecution to call for the Defence witness to be brought into its own exhibit. If you want to tender a Prosecution exhibit go ahead and do that and then leave the other one to the Trial Chamber to reconcile them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, I will have them allocated different numbers. I wanted to avoid the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It does not matter. If they are identical they will both go for the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases I will give them the separate number. There is not many more to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the point has been cleared and I think that is a better procedure, because I also wanted some clarifications in view of the differences of the translation that have been noted by my learned friend. In that case we would have to compare the translations too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In that event, I think without having to do this court, the other documents I have had married to Defence exhibits, if I may, with your Honour's leave, endeavour to do that during the break I will organise they be introduced as Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They have reasons for tendering particular exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am correcting the ones that have already gone in like that. The document of 14th August, 1992 now presently with the witness. Mr. Omerkic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise it as a genuine record of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it as a genuine document of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might this be given the next Prosecution number in order, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked Prosecutor document 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that document be removed from in front of the witness? The next document which will be given a Prosecution number was, however, admitted into evidence as Exhibit D77/1. Might I have the next number in order for Prosecution exhibits, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor document 201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you have copies for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I know we have got them, but go back again and then look them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is copied for your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I want now to see what the documents have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have the copies, even though it has been previously admitted. Mr. Omerkic, looking at that document that you have in front of you, do you recognise it as a genuine record of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it as a genuine record, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is a document that is kept in your archive, the original of which is kept in your archive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the original is kept in our archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that be admitted into evidence, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Exhibit 201 is admitted. I am not sure I remembered speaking to the admission of Exhibit 200. I am not too sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understood your Honour admitted it. If not I think the record is now clarified, your Honour, in relation to that. Might the exhibit in front of the witness now be removed and could he be shown the Bosnian version of the document I now hand to you. There are copies for the Defence and for your Honours. Might it be given the next Prosecution exhibit number in order? It has previously been made available to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor Exhibit 202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Exhibit 202 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases. The document Exhibit 202 which has been admitted into evidence, do you recognise that as a genuine record of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as is maintained in your archives, Mr. Omerkic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just look at it once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It does not relate to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object to the relevance of this document. It has nothing in common with the case we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At least one witness is mentioned here as a Colonel Divjak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I withdraw it your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we can break now and come back at 12.00. (11.30 am) (Short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would the Registrar kindly remind the witness that he is still on oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, that is the only question I had of this witness in relation to documents. I noted your Honour's comments about not having some documents married with Defence exhibits which I have done. I have not been able to unravel it now and determine which ones are which. I will have to correct that later, if we are to give them Defence exhibits one. There is no difficulty in the documents because they have been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your only responsibility is to present your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Because they were the same I was trying to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It may be confusing to take into account their own exhibit while tendering yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we can identify which ones they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We could. Because when the issues are gone into you find out which is relevant to what.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is all the questions I have of this witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Actually the view --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I address you? May I address you, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In what respect? I do not know what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not necessary for you to address your Honours on that. That document has been withdrawn, on a different basis; not because of whether it is from your archive but on the basis of its relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually your responsibility is to produce documents in your custody. Having produced that I think no questions are necessary about the documents themselves. You know nothing about the documents. All you know is that you keep them. I suppose this is all for the witness, except you want to ask him whether he has made any of these documents, whether he wrote them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe she has to prove certain documents of her own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you want to tender your own documents through him you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. Cross-examination by MS. RESIDOVIC

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Edina Residovic and I represent Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Pleased to meet you. I would first like to just give you information on the way we should proceed. I am going to ask you questions. Since we both speak Bosnian you would be able to very quickly respond to me. However, everything we say needs to be interpreted into one of the official languages, and taken down into the transcript. So please look, there is a headset, set of headphones on your right-hand side and there you can hear the interpretation of what I am asking you, so when you hear it finish then please respond. Very well. Is it correct what I am now going to ask of you? I am trying to figure out how many questions I need to ask you. You have responded to the question of the Prosecution that you can only authenticate those documents that are in your archive, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is correct is what I have compiled here in this list; and so everything that I have taken down and included in the list we have, and as I wanted to say about this document that was produced before it is not necessary. So if I can recognise certain elements so that there is a possibility that even though there may be problems in our archive, some documents got mislaid and things like that, but I can vouch for these that are on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that before you can answer my question regarding the authenticity you would have to look at the original document, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that if I showed you a document by the Supreme Commander, General Delic, that you would be able to testify to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could say that it looks similar to or something, but for these, I can say these are the originals and our army stands behind them. For anything you show me for that I could say this would be up to 99 per cent it looks like, it is similar to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind, you will be able to say that to the Trial Chamber when I show them to you. But is it correct that we can address either you or your Supreme Command for authentication of documents in your archive or to the archives in one of the corps? You would be able to authenticate these things? Would that be the correct way in which you identify certain documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anything that a person may need from our archives, they can get by the letter -- through a letter that General Delic issues to me. So I am a soldier and I report to General Delic, so General Delic is the person to go to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to facilitate our own work and the work of the Tribunal in general we do not need to discuss that now. We were told another person would be called in to authenticate certain documents. Is it true that you are only in possession of a small amount of documents controlled by the army of BiH and from the area of Konjic and of the 4th Corps, is it just a small amount?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably, yes, even though we did receive an order which we passed down to the lower levels. This was on the 27th of this month, so just two or three days ago. The deadline was set for part of the documents. So we received some of the documents but some of them were not processed correctly, so we returned them. And then some of it may have been returned back to us. So I do not know. We have to see whether it was processed properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, and I thank you for telling me as the counsel for Mr. Delalic how to proceed in order to get the documents that I need. Now I would like to proceed and show D75/1, this is evidence that has been already admitted. I would like to show it to the witness. Could you please tell me what you recognise in this document, of the characteristics that you told the Prosecutor confirm in your mind that this is an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, it is the stamp. It is similar, but I am not sure. The stamp is the first thing that I look at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an original stamp of the general staff of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also saw the signature of the Commander Rasim Delic. Is that the signature of the Commander Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure. I would even say that is rather not similar to his, but I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We will return the document and we will follow the procedure that the witness indicated. Since the witness was not able to review all the documents that the Defence has prepared I am not going to ask any further questions of him. Thank you. Your Honours, do I understand correctly that the documents offered by the Prosecution for authentication, and which had previously been submitted by the Defence, that all of them have been now confirmed as authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why are you asking that question? At the time it was tendered certain considerations were taken into account in admitting it. It is not the authenticity alone of the document at the moment it is being admitted into evidence. That could have been one of the considerations. Here what is being considered is whether the document which witness has identified as proceeding from his record. This is what happened here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you did not understand me fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I did. I could not, post fact to now, state that all those things were authentic. I could not say that after it had all been admitted on considerations other than the authenticity alone. What you are now asking is that now all documents which have been admitted into evidence on both sides have no reason to be regarded as authentic. This is why I am telling you that was not the only consideration for their being admitted, their relevance, their reliability, and their connection with the issue for which it is being tendered, all goes back to their admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is obvious that I did not ask the question properly. The large number of documents was only identified and today these documents were submitted by the Prosecutor to this witness as the custodian of the archives of the Bosnian Herzegovina for authentication. For instance, our evidence 77/1, 120, 131/1 were all identified today. At the request of the Prosecution they were identified and authenticated. I propose now that these documents be -- that were identified also be admitted, because they were identified as authentic documents by this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If he should have taken them as he did and they are identified as authentic documents they are admitted as such. They have their full value on the fact that they are consistent with the originals in his records. That is consistent with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I understood you correctly then, your Honour, that the documents whose authenticity was confirmed by this witness today that they are also admitted -- accepted as the evidence introduced by the Defence. I am sorry, this is the first time that I am involved in a case in which the process of identification is being handled in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is done while the witness is here. It has no further purpose than that. That is all we have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Other counsel might like to ask questions. Ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Any further cross-examination by any other counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, with your permission. Cross-examination by MR. OLUJIC

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. I would like to ask you several questions, but beforehand we need to clear up one matter; for the easier communication of my questions in the courtroom, since I speak Croatian and you speak Bosnian, please wait until the question has been interpreted into English and French, and only answer thereafter. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, during the examination-in-chief you said that you studied at the faculty of philosophy and that you studied library science, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was archival science a special subject of your study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that there is legislation in Bosnia-Herzegovina regarding archival work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the head of the archive department in the Ministry of the Defence do you have to respect that law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I need to add -- I also have to adhere to the provisional regulations that have been also added to this law and that has been signed by General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you have first of all have to adhere to these rules and regulations rather than the law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is a somewhat confusing question. Rules and regulations are framed under the law. I did not understand the question, that you have to adhere to rules and regulations rather than the law. Rules and regulations are framed under the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If counsel will be fair to the witness, you might put to him what that law is. It makes life easier for everyone, so that he will know what answers to give to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness said that he knew of this law of the archival work and that one should follow it, one should adhere to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The provisions you are relying upon which you want him to follow. He has told you he follows the regulations issued by General Delic. If you have other laws governing the regulations then tell him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The question was to follow. What I am interested in is whether you would adhere to the rules or to the law. Obviously the rules have to comply with the law. However, what I am interested in, sir, is in what period of time do you need to receive the documents that you request? In other words, is there a deadline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you will recall, I said that there was an order which regulated, and I do not know the date of it, the deadline for the production of all the archival material and this deadline has passed. However, there were some unexpected circumstances. There was a fire, there was the transformation of the army, certain signatures were no longer valid and there were new persons who arrived in new units to work on this archive, so there were -- we -- so we sent another document to all the units and requested that no further documents be delivered to us but that the work on its processing should continue, so that they would be prepared to send it to us. Also any request by anyone for any documents was also postponed because of the difficult circumstances. So this was force majeure, so we have to do it that way. I do not know if that is a satisfactory answer to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it is satisfactory. Thank you, Professor, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I address the court and may I add some further explanations in connection with this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. You may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to say that when talking about the education and training of archive keepers for the moment we have no such institution which would provide advanced training for custodians. As far as I remember, before the war in secondary school there would be a generation of people who would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Nobody is doubting your competency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- specialising in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I want to find out one thing. Can there ever be a deadline for the department of archives?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No deadline for receiving documents, whether any of your legislation has suggested a deadline for the receipt of documents into the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You receive documents of importance any time, even if it is 10 years later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The law, as far as I recall, does not set a definitive deadline by when the documents during the aggression need to be submitted. We are in a very difficult situation. It is very similar to the situation we had during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The deadline for the authorities to send the documents to you, not a deadline for you when you should receive them. The deadline would be for the department to send the document, it must be the departments or the general or the corps headquarters that they should send these papers to you within such and such a period. Anyway, it is not important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, your Honours, I should like to emphasise once again the date fixed by the order by which all the documents should have been submitted; but in the meantime these various things happened, like the fire in the building. So we cannot receive it in the room that we are sharing with the library, so we are living in a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understood you fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In the absence of further questions I think this witness is discharged. Thank you very much for your efforts in this matter and the zeal with which you explain your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was thinking of asking him some further questions about the process by which documents are acquired, but I think I will not. Instead I will talk about the frogs that have apparently rotten into the ceiling this morning. I hope it is not some Biblical plague that is being visited upon us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The frogs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It does not matter, as long as it finds its way into their collection. What else do you have, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is all the evidence we have available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness is discharged. You are discharged and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is all the evidence that -- excuse me -- that is all the evidence that we have available this week. We had estimated that with Professor Economides that we may have taken the full time. We have not done that. We can proceed to deal one by one with the documents that were obtained by the Austrian police which still have not been, as I understand it, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is -- as I understand it, there have been -- I was not quite sure of the nature of your Honours' orders, but if they have been accepted into evidence it is just a question of their establishing the relevance of them. It requires individual examination of them. We could do that. Later on this afternoon, if your Honours please, we could deal with the motion in relation to the UN officer and the Witness J for next week, or indeed that could be done next week, if your Honours please. It is entirely a matter for your Honours as to how you wish to proceed from now. We are in a position to look at the documents individually, if that is what your Honours would prefer. We have no further evidence at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why do you want to examine the UN security officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please let me take the questions. I have think you have indicated two things we have to do. The admission of the documents in the substantive case; now, what our ruling was, and very clearly, I thought you realised too, that what was tendered to us at that time were certain folders containing documents. What was received on the basis of their reliability and relevance are the folders not the contents of those folders. Now what you want to introduce now are the documents in the folders. We had no opportunity of knowing what those documents were to be able to consider whether in fact they could have been received at the time, the folders were tendered. Now, if you want to introduce the documents in the folders they have to be established on their own strength. They do not go with these folders themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do believe there is a confusion about this. Perhaps I will try to clarify it, if I may. There were some folders introduced, twelve folders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At no stage do we want to introduce into evidence the contents of those folders. We do not want to do it now, we did not want to do it then. The folders were merely introduced because they contained documents which before the folders ever got to this courtroom had documents in them which had been removed. Those documents that had been removed were addressed and examined individually by the witness Moerbauer and the witness Moerbauer said yes, this was a document we took out and he marked them and he gives certain evidence in relation to it. The documents that are contained now in those folders which are with the Registrar, we do not wish to tender them. There was only one purpose in introducing those folders and that was to show that these were the folders which contained the documents which had been removed prior to coming to court and were dealt with individually by the witness Moerbauer. The documents that I am now talking about are the documents that were examined individually by the witness Moerbauer, not the contents of the documents of the folders that I presented to your Honours at some subsequent stage. Now, it is possible that your Honours say that the documents that were individually dealt with by the witness Moerbauer have now been admitted into evidence, and the only outstanding issue is relevance. There are two ways we can deal with that. We can deal with it by making submissions individually on the documents now, or we can do it in closing address. I mean it does not have to happen at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are there any outstanding documents which have not been admitted into evidence for any purpose whatsoever? They might still be dealt with. But what our ruling was, that no documents because or by virtue of those folders were admitted at the time the folders were admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The contents of those folders, that is the documents contained in those folders were certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would not have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At that time. We do not seek to tender them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nobody is arguing that. This is not an argument before us, that the contents of the folders were not admitted. I think that is accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are not seeking to do that. But what we are seeking to do is to make sure that the documents that were not in the folders but were individually dealt with by Moerbauer have been accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours say that they have been admitted into evidence, then it is only an issue of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The contents, before they are admitted, have to be authenticated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just give you an example. In your office you keep so many files, maybe letters, maybe press cuttings. Some of them you do not believe to be true, some of them probably are false. If you take those documents without the contents being proved of those documents, as evidence, it will be unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the exercise that I am now in a position to go through and do, and individually indicate why we say: (a) the documents can be relied upon, (b) why they are relevant and why they should be admitted into evidence. The basis upon which I would seek to do that is by relating to the contents of the documents, where they were found, the circumstances of where they were found, and what they relate to. I can do that. That is done not only by the individual document as it stands alone but also in relation to the other documents with which it was contained because there is an inter-relationship between the documents. It is a process of showing that inter-relationship which then proceeds to demonstrate its authenticity and reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
