utterances.text: Supposing that letter, which is a forged one, is found on folders, the mere fact it was found in the folder, the folder has been recovered, the letter has been recovered, does not mean this letter is true. The contents of these documents have to be proved. Yes this document relates to a certain person. What you have done is proper custody, that this document has come from that custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not sure we are arguing the motion now. We are not arguing the issue. When you come properly we will argue the issue. I gave you the position of the Trial Chamber that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does your Honour wish me to address this by way of a motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well definitely, if it has not been admitted. You can raise it at any stage -- it need not be by motion -- but this is not the time to raise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The authenticity is very different from custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I know your Honour keeps saying that; and I never seem to be able to address your Honour on that point. Your Honours, a document -- you do not have to produce the author of the document for a document to be admitted into evidence, not so far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There are other considerations which might assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A document can be a printed document and still be relevant and admissible; but I do not need to produce the person who published the document or wrote it. A secretary could write a document about somebody. It is the contents of the document which is a factor. There are a number of ways to do it. You can do it by way of producing the person who wrote it, or you can look at the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, this is why there are two stages in the question of admissibility of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The first stage is the discovery of it, which we have done; and your Honours have accepted that, and custody; getting it here to the court, which is a relevant issue. The next stage, your Honours, is to look individually at the document and make a determination of the relevance and reliability based on the contents, and comparison with other documents. A document can speak about an event which if we know from other circumstances or other evidence did occur, tends to suggest that the document may be valid, because it says, "on X day I left Konjic and went somewhere else". If that is contained in the document and we have heard other evidence that says that, one says that probably is true. That is the process by which we need to go through each document to examine it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Supposing a document is found that I travelled to such and such place, maybe and I have never been to that place. What are you going to say to that? Unless there is some confirmatory evidence outside that document which shows it is genuine. An interview -- I have been the victim. So many interviews have been published about me, in Pakistan not here of course, which I never gave. If those documents are found; I kept a record, if they are found in my folder, would it mean that I have given that interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, and the reliability of the document, or the weight that is attached to it, is substantially reduced by evidence which suggests to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There has to be some other evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the documents can interrelate to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is a danger in that, that is why the contents of the document have to be proved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But they cannot be approved if the accused does not appear. The person who wrote them is the accused, and says "I refuse to testify" then those documents would never get into evidence. In my submission, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think there is a lot of cognitive evidence which might assist in its admissibility itself. But what you do with these documents as admitted would depend on the consideration the Trial Chamber places on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the end of the day, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I need to take your Honours to each document and interrelate it to other documents to explain the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Other documents which are in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Some are in evidence, but some are an inter-relationship between the documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have to show that all documents which are interrelated to each other are in evidence, for you to be able to establish what you are trying to prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a concept of admission de bene esse, where the documents are admitted and then examined, after they have admitted to their relevance. I mean, you may have a situation where the only way you can prove one document is by relation to another document. If you are not permitted to prove either document, because both of them are interrelated, then you never get the documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It can be very dangerous to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: De bene esse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not want to say that here. It is misconceiving the principle. Where evidence is reliable, even if the custody is also established, and all you need now is to determine whether in fact it should be used in evidence, you leave it to the Trial Chamber or the judge to determine from all the surrounding circumstances whether there is sufficient weight to be given to what has been tendered to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is all you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the exercise I think -- if your Honours do not need my assistance in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Of course we need your assistance in every matter related to this trial. How can we proceed without your assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Without knowing what you are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it would be necessary for your Honours for me to indicate to you why it is that we say that these documents are reliable. The only way I can do that is by looking at the documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are not doing it alone, you are doing it in conjunction with the Defence, who are entitled to object to whatever procedure you are trying to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Obviously, and at the end of the day it comes to a decision of your Honours, as I understand the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is why they should know what is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think they do. I think that they are very familiar with the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are not too sure. We are assuming as if everything is clear. Until we get to the roots of it, then we know what you are talking about, what circumstances you are talking about and in what respect you want the matter introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is why I have left the argument to this point, because we are reaching the closing stages of the Prosecution case. At an earlier stage, it is much harder to determine whether something is relevant than it is at this stage. We are at the very sunset of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can introduce it any time you wish to. We will listen to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I am in a position to proceed now if your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can you? Do you wish to do so now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can do it now if your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will listen to it. I am sure we can continue after lunch with this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first document that I would draw your attention to is exhibit 117; and the translation version of that is 117A.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If I may be heard. If we are to proceed on this, this has come without warning to us and we do not have our necessary documents to respond in kind to what the Prosecutor is going to attempt to do right now. Our understanding was that we were going to deal with the previous witness and that was all for the week. So we are a little bit surprised and not in a position to respond document by document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am sure each document will be tendered to you. If you have any observations you can make them. They are not documents with which you are so unfamiliar that you cannot say anything about them. You are quite familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before you proceed further, I asked you a question but then another matter took up. Why do you produce a UN security officer? Why do you want to examine a UN security officer, because we had some probe people claiming privilege, UN employees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this question is being addressed by my colleague Ms. McHenry, and I might ask her in fact to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can do that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can indicate, your Honours, very quickly, that the evidence that this witness would give is something that the Defence have raised themselves in a motion by Ms. McMurrey relating to evidence coming before the Chamber pursuant to a process other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This relates to that motion by Landzo, I see. We can discuss it when that motion comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is why I am calling the evidence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am sorry for this interruption, because I thought the thing will remain in my mind because I had that privilege question. At some stage in these proceedings, in some other matter it was said that UN employees cannot come without the claim -- they had some sort of privilege. I had that in my mind. I am sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the matter raised by Mr. O'Sullivan, if they would be assisted by us adjourning now and them getting their documents ready so we can proceed this afternoon I think I have no objection to that. I think it is fair so that they can gather their materials together. I can understand why they may have been taken a little by surprise. If they can come back this afternoon at 2.30 and we can proceed then. Certainly I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not you now, it is their privilege. It is not you objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I know that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that suitable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, that will be fine, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. So we will have a break and then come back at 2.30. (12.55 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you are continuing with your submissions, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, as I had indicated earlier, the only effective way I think that I can demonstrate the relevance, the significance of each of these documents is by going to the documents themselves and pointing out the various facets of the document and stating why it is that I submit that they are relevant. The first document that I would ask your Honours to --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object at this point. I ask to be heard on this. My starting point is this: that as your Honours pointed out before the break that in your ruling of September 12th you held that the folders were admissible but not the contents of those folders. My learned friend now is seeking to lead into evidence items coming allegedly from INDA-BAU, all of which were contained in the folders I1 through I12. He seems to be under the misconception that there are documents which were not contained in folders. When Officer Moerbauer came here his testimony was he received the twelve folders from his colleagues. No one at that point to handing the folders over to the police station had anyone marked those documents contained in those twelve folders. Officer Moerbauer's testimony further stated between 22nd March to approximately April 2nd he opened the folders and marked the documents. Third, when Officer Moerbauer testified before this Tribunal he was shown the documents my friend is now attempting to admit into evidence; and Officer Moerbauer could not identify his mark on any documents. There was no connection between what Officer Moerbauer said he did in Vienna and the documents that were shown here. The Prosecution has not proven the authenticity of these documents; they are therefore unreliable. We cannot move on to the next step. We do not know the provenance of these documents. The Prosecution has failed to prove that. I repeat, I heard my friend this morning say that he is talking about documents which were not in folders. That is not correct. The record is clear. All of these documents, allegedly from INDA-BAU, were contained in these twelve folders. That is the testimony of Moerbauer himself. He received them unmarked; he marked them. When he came here there were no markings put on those documents by Moerbauer. That is the threshold question, in my submission, which has not been proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: For the record, we support that contention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are documents now contained in the twelve folders. Those documents are in the twelve folders that are now in the twelve folders we do not seek to tender. Documents were taken out of the folders and dealt with separately before the twelve folders were tendered. They were individually considered by Mr. Moerbauer. Mr. Moerbauer considered each one and commented on each one individually. In relation to the first document that I am seeking to deal with, Exhibit 117, Mr. Moerbauer said, at page 3652, lines 1 to 8: "I made an index myself of the seized items and here I can locate the exact binder. This document was in binder 12. The document was handed to me by my colleague Mr. Navrat in the binder at the police headquarters in Vienna." In relation to each one of these documents I deal with, Mr. Moerbauer specifically dealt with them in this way. There seems to be either a complete confusion in the minds of the Defence about this or that they just refuse to accept what I am saying. I think I have made myself very clear as to what the position is. These documents are documents that came out of the binder and were dealt with by Moerbauer before the binders were tendered. There is no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is this document 117?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is a draft of a letter found at the premises of INDA-BAU in handwriting. It is in draft form and it contains references to such matters as the fact that up until the 25th November, 1992, the document said, "I was in the war 24 hours a day without a day's rest or break or change", and goes on and talks about, "in July I was appointed the commander of Tactical Group 1." It goes on with the establishment of the 4th Corps in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The contention seems to be that not all the documents seized were in the folders as were tendered, is that your contention?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The contention, your Honour, is it is not a contention, your Honour, what happened is that we took certain of the documents which we considered to be relevant out of the folders and introduced them into evidence individually, one by one. Those documents were dealt with by Mr. Moerbauer one by one. He then gave evidence in relation to them and said that this particular document comes from folder number so and so, and I receive the folder from Mr. Navrat. All of this evidence of chain has been given. Your Honours have ruled on it. Your Honours have decided that the evidence is admissible insofar as the seizure of the documents, the chain of evidence of how it got to it. The only issue remaining is the question of whether it is relevant and probative and whether it should be admitted into evidence on that basis. Any arguments about any other matter, your Honour, in my submission, have been dealt with, and it is improper to raise those issues again which have already been litigated. This will go on forever if this happens, which is what the Defence seem to wish to do. They refuse to accept that your Honours have made a ruling on this question. Your Honours have ruled on it. The only issue now outstanding is the question of relevance. Quite rightly, your Honours have said whether or not they will be admitted into evidence depends upon whether they can shown to be relevant, which is what I am seeking to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If I might be heard on this point. My intention, quite to the contrary to what my learned friend says, is not to waste time. I respectfully submit there is another portion of evidence that must be considered which is fatal to the admissibility of these evidence. Officer Moerbauer says he analysed and put his mark on every document that was in folders I1 to I12. When he came before this Tribunal to give evidence he did not see his mark on any document coming from those folders. There is no connection between what he said he did in Vienna and what he testified to in this courtroom in regards to these documents. That is the threshold question of authenticity and reliability. So I am not trying to waste time. My submission is that that evidence is fatal to proving the first point, which is the authenticity and reliability of these questions. That should close the matter once and for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, your Honours, this is a refusal to accept your Honours' orders, which it would seem my friend refuses to accept. I mean, your Honours have already ruled on this question. Mr. Moerbauer has looked at these documents and identified them as documents that he received. Your Honours have accepted that. There is no question about that. I cannot understand why, this issue that they are attempting to relitigate this question again. It is a question now of the relevance. They keep on wanting to raise the issues of what Moerbauer did, how the documents were handled, the chain and the whole issue of their seizure. Your Honours have ruled on that. The only question is the question of their relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Again, if I am not making myself understood, I am not asking to relitigate anything, I am asking the Tribunal to look at the record and to apply your ruling of September 12th, where you said the contents of the folders is not admitted. Then we can raise objections to the individual documents as the Prosecution attempted to have them brought into evidence. The evidence is clear. The officer who seized the documents from INDA-BAU, Navrat, did not mark them. They were marked for the first time, according to Moerbauer, between 22nd March and 2nd April. Those documents arrived in this courtroom with no marks. In my respectful submission, there is no proof those are the same documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, Professor, let us get this clear. If your contention is that anything which was not admitted in the contents of the folders, this was what was said, the contents were not admitted, what do you have against it being subsequently admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could prove it, it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You will hear the Prosecution first, because I do not see the objection if what is being argued is that although it might have been indicated as not being admitted, it is now being submitted for admission. You also put up your argument against why it should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There is no proof that exhibit number 117 was in folder number I2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the more reason why it should now be brought for admission if it was not there, if all that was admitted were matters which were not in the folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Moerbauer says it was in the folder and when pressed if he could recognise the mark he said he put on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The context. We do not even know what are the contents of the folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Officer Moerbauer says he marked the contents with his mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The contents have not been tendered to us. There is no list of what are the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The evidence is that Moerbauer says he marked the contents of I2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I would prefer you listening to the argument first and put up your argument. It appears you are starting on the very wrong premise. The argument is what you are saying is that the contents of the folder were not admitted. This was what you said. We do not even know what the contents of the folder is. How do you now posit any argument about it being admitted unless you can show that what is now being suggested has been rejected?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The threshold question, in my submission, is proving that the document was in I2, that was the same document that Moerbauer saw in Vienna and could not identify in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not see any substance in the argument. Let me hear Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What I rely on, your Honour, is that extract of the evidence that I read out, where Moerbauer said in evidence at 3652, lines 1 to 8: "This document was in binder 12. This document was handed to me by my colleague, Mr. Navrat, in the binder at the police headquarters in Vienna." So in each case it was dealt with. So, your Honours, in my submission it is incorrect for the Defence to be saying that there is no evidence of where the document came from or that there is no evidence that Moerbauer knew where the document came from and was able to identify that. He did. The evidence is here. It is clear, and he says so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does it show it was in the -- the mere fact it was found at INDA-BAU is sufficient to show it is in the handwriting of Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He does not say that he does not know what the handwriting is like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually that is the second stage for the admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is. It is the second stage with respect to the extent to which the Prosecution says the document should be used. If it is to go to prove an element of the offence it would be incumbent to prove that it was in his handwriting and something he himself says is to be used against him. A document can be about somebody, it does not have to be written about him, it still becomes relevant. It can be written by anybody else and it is still relevant. The indicia of reliability, where did it come from, is it in a place where somebody would expect it to be. If you find it in a garbage tin in the middle of Berlin you could say, how could it be relied upon in any way. If you find it in premises which are occupied and where the business of the accused is then the indicia of reliability increases. All these factors go together to establish this indicia of reliability. At the end of the day, your Honours may not say that this one particular document will prove the matter beyond a reasonable doubt. It may go to the proof of the matter along with a lot of other pieces of evidence. The fact that a wallet is found on a premises may not prove that it is the wallet of the person, but if it has in its contents a licence which says the licence of this person and a credit card and so forth the combination of all these factors tend to show that this may have belonged to Mr. X. The fact that it is found on these premises may suggest that Mr. X may have been on these premises at a particular time. It is a combination of factors. It is called circumstantial evidence. All I am submitting, your Honours, is that we are putting these documents in for these purposes. They are going to have varying degrees of weight. Some will have greater weight than others. Unless your Honours seek to rely on them, at the end of the day, to prove, the one document to prove conclusively an element, you might require it to be of a very high standard of proof. The fact that it is not of the highest standard of proof, such that it is proved to be in the handwriting of the individual, does not make it inadmissible. It means that the weight that you attach to it is reduced, because of the fact that it is not shown to be in that handwriting, not proved to be in that handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All you can say is that this document indicates that the accused was holding these positions at the relevant time, that is all. It has been found in his possession, this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may say something relevant about the accused, such as, if -- we have been speaking of CVs in the last few days. Very few of us actually, in handwriting which we would prove in court, write out our CVs. Most of the time it is done by our secretaries. It is not suggested that because it is done by the secretary that it is not relevant to us. One looks at the contents. It says you are born on a certain date and that can be proved otherwise that it is consistent with it, that it relates to a particular academic qualification and so forth all the way through, you may say this document looks like it may be the CV of X. It does not have to be proved I wrote it or it was written by anyone in particular to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, please can I make a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In opposition, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to offer the opposite argument. I think that the Prosecutor is trying to take us further away from the decision of the Trial Chamber, since the Officer Moerbauer recognised some of the documents from the folders, from the transcript I think that is not true. I think that in his analysis compiled a month and a half after the seizure of certain items he analysed certain documents and he could only speak to those. In the folders he only recognised to a single document which allegedly was found in the -- Mr. Delalic's apartment. And the Prosecutor just said they were not going to use any documents from the folders found on the premises of Mr. Delalic. Witness Moerbauer has testified here that no document in these folders is -- he cannot recognise because he does not speak good Bosnian language, because he never submitted the documents for the graphological analysis and in no other way can ascertain where the documents came from. The only thing that happened was that the witness Navrat gave him these documents. That witness who was on the premises in INDA-BAU could not recognise a single document, who was in those folders, because he put no markings on any of these documents. He could not read any of these documents, and no documents there was ever written to him. So the fact that the Prosecution is claiming that the documents from INDA-BAU are from the premises of Mr. Delalic go counter to all evidence that we have -- testimony that we have heard here. Mr. Moerbauer, this firm INDA-BAU was always the ownership -- was never the ownership of Mr. Delalic. He never worked there. There are 300 employees there, but Mr. Delalic was never there. So the witness who appeared before the Tribunal did not recognise anything, and now the arguments that are being put forward and the documents are being offered here that nobody has ever recognised I think are trying to mislead this court, and in the letter I think that I have showed that there were two letters and my defendant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, was any of the contents of the folders tendered during argument?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They are being tendered now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We are not denying the right, however, for the Prosecution first has to prove that they were in the INDA-BAU folders, and the Prosecution has offered no evidence in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I find it amazing that they keep saying we have not offered the evidence. I just quoted twice, and I will quote again. Moerbauer, at page 3652 of the transcript, in dealing with the first document that I wish to deal with, says: "I made an index myself of the seized items and here I can locate the exact binder. This document was in binder 12." That is Exhibit 117. It was in binder 12: "This document was handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, in the binder at the police headquarters in Vienna." Why do the Defence refuse to accept this? It is the evidence. It has been proved. The evidence is before the court and yet I find it extraordinary that no matter the fact I have mentioned it three times they refuse to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I may be able to be of a little bit of assistance here. I think we have two people talking past each other, that there is conflicting evidence. I think each side is saying our evidence shows, because we presented evidence, shows the court made a fact-finding on this piece of evidence where the Prosecution would say that there was testimony that it came from here, and then the Defence would say he testified that he put marks on all of the documents, and he could not find a mark on this document so it could not be the same document. I think at some point the Trial Chamber is going to have to make a fact-finding here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They are not talking about the same matter. It appears they are not saying the same things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think it would require a detailed examination of all the evidence, whether this particular document was found at the premises or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Defence case is there is no evidence that this document was one of the documents recovered from INDA-BAU. The Prosecution thinks there is enough evidence. It requires a detailed examination of the entire evidence and maybe at this stage it is not possible to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All through there was no detailed examination of the documents in the folders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Clearly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nobody, so if today somebody at that time one would have insisted we should have the documents in these folders, then you could have excluded any subsequent tendering of evidence as being claimed to be belong to any of these folders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think that Rule 89E may be the solution to this problem, which -- I believe it is Rule 89E, which suggests that if there is a -- yes, 89E, when it comes to authenticity of evidence the Trial Chamber can ask for more. I think what you have here is conflicting evidence, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are clearly not in conflict because they are all speaking at cross-purposes. One says, "I removed this from the folders". The other says no such thing ever happened. That is speaking at cross-purposes. If all the folders were admitted minus their contents, obviously the contents were not in issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. And now you can go forward to show what the contents are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think the conflicting evidence is this: Moerbauer says this is my -- I took what was it 114, 117, this is one I took out of this folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: "And I put a mark on it. I put a mark on everything I took out of there", and later he says, "no, I cannot find the mark".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Cannot identify the mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It should have my mark on it and I cannot find it. I think perhaps the Trial Chamber -- at some point is going to have to make a fact-finding. Rule 89E may be what the Trial Chamber might want to use to get some more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, are you still ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague Mr. Niemann says that he is surprised that we are not hearing the arguments. I think that the testimony of a witness provides the answers, during his examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. During the cross-examination the same witness denied everything that Mr. Niemann is referring to. He did not recognise a single document except for the letter, "Dear Edine", which allegedly comes from the department of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. As for all the other objects, he could not identify them. Therefore, your Honours, we do not know what was in those folders. If the Prosecution wishes to tender them then they first have to prove that they were there in the first place and then I am sure additional evidence would have to be sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I wonder if I can just raise two matters your Honour, with your Honour's kind leave. Your Honour, the reason why this problem has arisen may come from your Honours' words on 12th September. I am going to read them back to you, if you will forgive me: "We have observed that the Defence is entitled to address the Trial Chamber on those issues and will be entitled to challenge the admissibility of any documents sought to be tendered as arising from the search or discrepancies from evidence of witnesses. This is because the Prosecution is seeking to tender 12 folders containing documents but not the documents". Your Honour, that may be where the intention that we are entitled to raise this matter comes from. That is the first matter. The second matter is this: my learned friend Mr. Niemann, in discussing the question of admissibility of documents, said this: a document can be about somebody, it does not have to be about him. I think he may have said by him. It can be written by anybody else and it is still relevant. Your Honour, if there is a document which is written by who knows, who is not a witness in the case, perhaps even by a fellow defendant who cannot be forced to give evidence, there would, in my submission, admitting such documents on that basis be a fundamental breach of Article 21 and the provisions entitling someone to a fair trial. In particular, 21(4)E, the right to examine and have examined witnesses against him, because this person giving this account about a defendant is not before the court and it is a backdoor way of getting in evidence which is not going to be subject to cross-examination. In my respectful submission, my learned friend's premise that he makes there is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually my surprise here is that all that has been happening from the bench of the Defence is completely against the rules of debate. I expect if the Prosecution is making a submission about tendering evidence you listen to him and oppose it. You refused to listen to him irrespective of the fact that he is referring to aspects of the proceedings which he participated in. As has been read out even by Mr. Greaves, what we said that the contents of the -- of the folders which have been tendered were not also admitted and you are entitled to oppose that. But now you have not even heard his contents yet you are opposing them. In fact you are refusing argument on them. That is most irregular. I have never had such a thing. You listen to an argument and then put up your own arguments against it. You do not say that the opponent is stopped from even putting up an argument. There is nothing which stops him, because these matters have not been admitted, has not been rejected. So why would he not make his own argument in support of what he wants to and then you oppose it in the normal rules of argument?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, two more sentences, if I may. I fully support what you have just said and I understand that the Prosecutor is entitled to present the arguments. But the first argument was to offer a document saying that it was in one of the folders. I draw attention to page 3754 and 3755.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you please listen to him? When he finishes you tell him that it is not in one of the folders and you put up your own argument. I think that is the pattern that I am familiar with. Many of the things that the opposition say might be irritating, but you listen and then put up your own arguments. Let us hear Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. Your Honour, the first document that I wish to refer to is Exhibit 117, and so that we may all know which document we are talking about, I ask that the English version of that document be displayed on the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is very small print. I do not know if you can decipher it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can it be made larger, perhaps just the top part of it? That is it, thank you. If your Honours please, the original version of this document, which the Prosecution contend was recovered from the premises at INDA-BAU and was contained in the folder, and I should say I2, I have been saying 12 previously, I apologise for that, I2, is a hand-written document. In our submission, your Honour, the document contains a number of factors which we submit go to the question of its authenticity and reliability. There are indicia of -- there are indicia of reliability contained in the document itself. Your Honours, firstly, in the first paragraph of the document, it makes reference to, "an unspeakably widespread and unrelenting campaign waged against me". Your Honours have heard evidence from General Pasalic in relation to the question of the fact that he instigated proceedings against Mr. Delalic concerning his involvement and departure from the Konjic area. There are other documents that I have contained in this list, which go to that particular issue and which in particular were considered by General Pasalic during the course of the giving of his evidence. In particular, your Honours, Exhibit 137, and might the original version of 137 in -- sorry, might the English translation of 137 be displayed on the screen? This, your Honours is an exhibit. It is not -- it is a document that was recovered at the premises. It was recovered at the premises of INDA-BAU. It was referred to by the witness Moerbauer in his evidence, and in relation to that. The witness Moerbauer said, at page 3655, lines 1 to 3 of the transcript: "This document was in binder 18 and was also handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, at Vienna police headquarters." Your Honour, this document which is admitted into evidence makes reference to the fact that a number of persons, on the recommendation of General Pasalic, were to be detained for a period of 30 days; and in particular, at the very bottom, the fourth numbered paragraph at the very bottom, says: "Issue an arrest warrant by MUP BiH Interpol for Zejnil Delalic, Commander of TG1", et cetera. In my submission, your Honours, this Exhibit 137, goes, in my submission, to the question of whether or not a campaign may or may not have been being waged against him. The reason I say that it has an indicia of reliability is because a person in the position of Mr. Delalic, when hearing of these charges being raised against him, may well speak of it in terms such as this. I go on, your Honours. In the third paragraph of this particular document there is a reference there to: "From that time until 25th November 1992 I was in the war for 24 hours a day." Your Honours, you again heard the evidence of General Pasalic in relation to the time when it is said by him that the accused left the Konjic area and for a time at least General Pasalic was saying he did not know where the accused was. Your Honours, the document numbered 124, Exhibit 124, in particular on the -- in particular on the first page in the third paragraph there is what I would submit is a reference to that particular incident that was referred to by General Pasalic in his evidence, where it says: "In the course of the day on 25th November 1992 I was warned that someone close to me would try to kill me." Now, in my submission, your Honours, there has been evidence heard that the accused, Mr. Delalic, was concerned for his life at that particular time. That was offered by him as a reason as to why he left the Konjic area at the time that he did. In my submission, your Honours, this document, document 117, when read in conjunction with 125 -- sorry, 124 -- tends to show that the reference there to that date is something which is written about the accused. It may well have been written by the accused Delalic but is certainly consistent with the other evidence that your Honours have heard. If I go on to the second paragraph, the -- sorry, the next paragraph of Exhibit 117, if we can go back to that please, Exhibit 117, and go to the next paragraph, it starts: "In July", at the very top of your Honours' screen, "I was appointed the Commander of Tactical Group 1, which co-ordinated the army forces in the wider area of northern Herzegovina, central Bosnia, as far as Mount Igman." Your Honours have heard evidence on the question of who, in July, was appointed the Commander of Tactical Group 1. Your Honours, the document, the Exhibit 118 is a document that I believe your Honours have seen, and if that could be placed on to the screen, please, and if it could be made as large as possible, thank you. The English version of that document is a document which appears to be signed by the chief of the armed forces of the main staff, a gentlemen called Sefer Halilovic. Your Honours have heard evidence from General Pasalic in relation to the role played by the Chief of Staff whose name was given to you as Sefer Halilovic. Your Honours know from the evidence that this was a gentlemen who was in a position as Chief of Staff to control the various operations of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that period of July of 1992. Your Honour will see from this document, Exhibit 118, that it says, "I hereby appoint Zejnil Delalic to the post of commanding officer of the BiH army Tactical Group 1 for the area of Hadzici, Pazaric, Konjic and Jablanica." In my submission, your Honours, this reference here, having regard to all of the evidence that you have heard in relation to Tactical Group 1 and the responsibilities of the accused, Zejnil Delalic, would tend to suggest that this reference is -- this document is a reliable document, a document that your Honours could consider as relating to the accused. In my submission, your Honour, the fact that it was found on the premises of INDA-BAU, a premises where the Austrian police attested to the fact that they saw the accused leave those premises a day or so before, is further evidence that he was there, and I will take you to a subsequent document later on which in my submission will indicate that this accused did in fact have a connection with that premises. Your Honours, at the very bottom paragraph on page 1 of this document, in the English version of it, there is -- and perhaps if that could be shown on the screen, that is Exhibit 117, the very bottom paragraph if you please, thank you. It says: "With the establishment of the 4th Corps, Mostar and the 1 Sarajevo Corps already established, my former zone of responsibility was covered. So in the middle of November it was concluded that TG1 would be dissolved." Your Honours have heard a great deal of evidence about from General Pasalic and others about the creation of the 4th Corp. General Pasalic attested to the fact that the 4th Corps took over responsibilities of all of these areas and it was because General Pasalic, as Commander of the 4th Corps, took over this particular area that he was empowered or authorised to conduct an investigation into the events that occurred in Konjic and in the Celebici camp. So in my submission, your Honour, this is yet a further indicia of reliability of this document and would, in my submission, tend to suggest that it was a document written either about this accused or by this accused. It says: "From the moment that my duties were practically taken over by these corps and finally I catch my breath and go on a long-awaited visit abroad." It then makes reference, your Honour, to the deputy. I will come back to that later. The second page, if your Honour pleases, of this document, and in the top paragraph of the second page, the first full sentence that appears there, it says that: "I believe that on 20th November, 1992, I made a recommendation to the main staff for Colonel Arif Pasalic" -- the very man that your Honour has heard testify -- "to be made Commander of the 4th Corps, which was accepted. That is why I still have not fully comprehended some of his moves following my departure." Your Honours, in my submission, that could not be clearer. It relates clearly, in my submission, to the fact that General Pasalic took the steps that he did to have Zejnil Delalic arrested, and one would expect that if indeed the accused, Zejnil Delalic, did recommend that General Pasalic be appointed as Commander to the 4th Corps, which was accepted, he may be mystified, distressed and disturbed that after having taken that step, which was a step towards the promotion of General Pasalic, that it turns around that he commences an investigation against him, and may well be good reason why he would write: "That is why I still have not fully comprehended some of his moves following my departure." Again, I submit, your Honour, that these are further indicia of reliability. The next sentence says: "Persons who knew about any travel plans were first of all Colonel Pasalic." There may be some dispute between the accused Zejnil Delalic and Pasalic in relation to this question, but it seems that there is at least some aspect of this that might be correct, because you heard General Pasalic attest to the fact that he did take steps to warn the accused about travelling through various parts of Herzegovina at that relevant time. The next paragraph, your Honours, again makes reference to that date, that important date, in my submission, the 25th November, and again makes reference to the fact that an attempt was made upon his life. He then speaks, in the next paragraph, the author of this document then speaks, in the next paragraph, "at about 8 pm on 25th November we left" and then gives the route by which they left. Then says: "In Zagreb we had breakfast at 8 am in a splendid restaurant. At 10 am I continued the trip to Austria" -- Austria, bear in mind, is where the offices of INDA-BAU are located: "At the border crossing Spilfeld I even typed the date '26th November' in passport", which disproves all those fancy fabrications about helicopters and other nonsense. Your Honour has heard evidence about helicopter escapes, how it was said that the accused, Zejnil Delalic, had defected to the Serbs and had been picked up in a helicopter and flown off to somewhere in Serb hill territory which he denied, which again, in my submission, is being denied here with the use of the words "disproves all those fancy fabrications about helicopters". Your Honours, the document Exhibit 144, at page 7 of that document, if we could go to page 7 and it is the paragraph third from the bottom, if that could be highlighted for me, please. Your Honours, I wish to take you to the very last sentence there in that paragraph, starting with the words, it is the top one as you see on your screen, the sentence starting: "The staff of splendid restaurant knew me well and welcomed me warmly. We continued on our way to Maribel at about 1000 hours. The Croatian side checked my passport on computer and the Austrian stamped the date of my crossing, 26th November, 1992 at Spilfeld". As we know, helicopters do not land in Spilfeld, particularly not Chetnik ones. Again, I submit to your Honours that this is further evidence of the authenticity and reliability of this document. Going back, your Honour, to document 117, if I may, and to the second page that we were considering before, and to the one sentence, paragraph in the very middle of the page, if that could be highlighted please. That sentence appears at the bottom of your Honours' screen, it says : "In Vienna I was met by a large group of enthusiastic sympathisers, family and business friends." Your Honours, there is a reference, then, to the fact that he made contact in the next paragraph, the fact that he made contact with associates in Konjic and indeed, in my submission, the documents will show that contact was made back, especially with the deputy. There is a reference under the second question, which is the second last paragraph on that page, to a conversation with Colonel Jovan Divjak, a person that your Honours have heard from in the course of the evidence. It says, interestingly, that: "I saw and talked to Colonel Jovan Divjak when he appeared in Konjic in mid-October as the first member of the main staff who managed to leave Sarajevo." Your Honours will recall Colonel Divjak testifying to the fact that he had travelled by taxi, he had left Sarajevo and then he made his way, ultimately and finally arrived in Konjic. He also spoke of the time when he was there and he also spoke of meeting the accused, Zejnil Delalic. In my submission, those matters again are matters which go to show the authenticity. If we go over to the third page, your Honours, please. At the top of the page it says: "My colleagues have been detained without any legal basis and those who organised it have not even issued orders for detention", et cetera. Again, I submit that this is a reference to the fact that not only did General Pasalic seek to detain and question and ultimately commence legal proceedings against, if that was the result of the investigation, not just one person but a number of persons, those persons were mentioned by General Divjak in the Exhibit 137, which I have taken your Honours to and we know that the accused, by the evidence, was related -- had association with some of those persons, such that he may well refer to them as his "colleagues". Your Honours, then there is a reference in the next, fourth question, it is said, the final paragraph: "As regards requiring material benefit, it is exactly the opposite. Just in brief, I am offering 10,000 Deutsch Marks reward to anyone who can confirm a name, headquarters or person to whom I have sold anything or from whom I have taken even one Dinar, Deutsch Marks or the like." Your Honours, in document 124, at page 3, and it is the top paragraph of that document, could that be highlighted for me please, just the very top. Your Honours will see in about the centre of that paragraph, the following words: "I will offer a reward of 10,000 German Marks to anybody who can prove that I have sold a single gun, bullet or anything else to anyone. On the contrary, at the start of the war I mortgaged two large family, fully furnished houses and invested over a million German Marks to buy all sorts of things from weapons and vehicles to fuel, hand-held radios and signal systems, including 2,000 uniforms." In my submission, your Honours, having regard to the fact that this document, Exhibit 117, was, in our submission, found on the premises of the accused at INDA-BAU, it was referred to by Mr. Moerbauer as a document that was contained in binder 12. That it has all this indicia of reliability makes it not only relevant and probative but sufficiently reliable and should be admitted into evidence, and I move that it be admitted and accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any reaction from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. I repeat, witness Moerbauer, in the course of the cross-examination, on page 3754 and 3755, said clearly in this court that he could not recognise any one of the documents in the binders because they did not contain his mark, except for one document beginning "Dear Edine", which allegedly comes from Zejnil Delalic's apartment. For those reasons the court rightly asked the Prosecutor to bring witnesses who would be able to recognise the documents, that is the people who actually seized those documents in INDA-BAU. Witness Navrat, who did the search in INDA-BAU, was not able to confirm the authenticity of any one of these documents in the binders. He only confirmed the colour of the binders shown to him. Therefore, the ruling of the court and the efforts of the Prosecution to prove that these documents were in INDA-BAU premises through the witness were not proven. Navrat, Panzer and the other witnesses from Austria showed clearly that INDA-BAU is not owned by Mr. Delalic and that from its beginning to the present day Mr. Zejnil Delalic never worked in that firm. Therefore, the connection between Mr. Delalic and those premises does not exist. The Prosecutor, trying to link this document with the facts inside with some other testimony heard by this court, wishes to indicate its reliability and authenticity. I draw attention to the court that this is a document written in handwriting, that it has no date, that it is not signed, that we are trying to bring into evidence a document that was allegedly found on 18th March, 1996 in Vienna, merely because my client did in fact in November 1992 leave Konjic and go to Vienna. This is an undisputed fact, which the Prosecutor has already proven in the court and which has been confirmed by many witnesses, cannot retroactively be applied to a document found four years later, in order to assert the reliability of that document. Therefore, your Honours, offering an analysis of this document whose handwriting we do not know, no one has recognised it. It has not been signed. It is not dated, and asking that it be admitted, we are being placed in completely -- in a situation which we cannot understand at all. There are also facts that the Prosecutor could prove through the passport of Mr. Delalic or through Mr. Arif Pasalic. We are putting in a situation for a document to be admitted then in the future on the basis of such an unreliable document another document may be admitted. Unfortunately, I have never had such an experience before. You, your Honours, have much more, so I may be wrong. I think that bearing in mind the testimony of Mira Panzer and Navrat we cannot confirm the origins, the source of this document, who signed it, when it was signed. It is absolutely unreliable, regardless of the fact it refers to, and I feel that it cannot be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will consider it and perhaps give a ruling early next week some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases. Your Honours, the next document that I ask to be displayed on the screen is document 118. In relation to the document 118 that now appears on your Honours' screen, I have shown your Honours this document in the course of the submission I made in relation to Exhibit 117. In relation to this document, Mr. Moerbauer said this was also in binder 13, "was handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, at the Vienna police headquarters after the house search, at Koppstrasse 14." Your Honours, this document was shown to the accused, Mr. Delalic, by my colleague Ms. McHenry during the course of an interview on 22nd and 23rd August of 1996. At that stage, when the document was shown he said: "No, there was another document that was written earlier than this one. That document is dated 11 July, but I received that document after I received this one, so that one is not valid." In my submission, your Honour, there is no suggestion in the response that the accused gave that this is not a document that was found in the premises and not a document that necessarily relates to him. He does, however, I readily admit, does however say that this is not the only one, that there were two documents. That does not in any way go to the question of whether or not it was a proper document relating to him. It certainly does not address the concern of the Defence that it was a document that was not found on the premises. This document, however, has, in my submission, been admitted into evidence. It has been admitted into evidence as an annex to the record of interview itself, Exhibit 99, so it is not necessary for me to move for its admission. But the reason I am referring to it specifically is because of the inconsistency that is created by the suggestion of the Defence that the Prosecution has no way proved where these documents come from and that therefore, because we have failed to do that, that they should not be admitted into evidence. It is ironic indeed that when the accused is confronted with this document he does not say, "this is not a document of mine, where did you find it?", and reject it on that basis. No, he merely questions the date of it and raises the fact there was another document which he says is more relevant to the issue. I further say, your Honours, that the Defence counsel have admitted on numerous occasions that INDA-BAU was the accused Delalic's business, and as said in the record of interview, he agreed with this particular document. I go on, your Honours, to the next document which is exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the Defence say something in connection with the reliability of the evidence offered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the Defence has never stated that Delalic was the owner of INDA-BAU. Delalic worked in INDA-BAU in Munich and the Prosecutor has the appropriate evidence of this. He did not work in INDA-BAU, Vienna. Secondly, since my learned colleague Ms. McHenry is in the courtroom who also showed the document, dated 11 July, 1992, to my client in the course of his interrogation in Scheveningen, and in my presence, I must say that that is precisely proof of the unreliability of the evidence being offered to prove that the documents were found in Vienna. These are documents that were shown to the witnesses Pasalic and Divjak. This is a document regarding his appointment of 11 July, 1992, found in Munich and not in Vienna, and which at the top indicates the fax number, INDA-BAU, 23rd July 1992, to allege that my client was shown a document from Vienna can easily be disproved by insight into the statement of my client and his comment indicating why the date of 23rd July is there, and during hearing these witnesses and especially the Generals, the court has been able to see what the difficulties were in the communication between the Supreme Staff and the ground forces, how difficult it was to deliver appointments, orders and other documents from Sarajevo into the field and the court was able to establish that all communications with foreign countries by messengers et cetera, how difficult they were, and sometimes lives were risked to get a message to its destination. There is no doubt that my client was shown this document from Munich, and on that document the fax number is indicated and the date, and Munich. This document that is now being offered as evidence to prove that he was shown a document from Vienna is illustrative of the unreliability of all the documents found in those folders. Therefore, we do not object to this document which is attached to the statement, but it is not the document that it is purported to be. There is no reliable proof to show that this document of 11th July was in any one of the folders which the witnesses recognised in this courtroom and which were found in the INDA-BAU company. In fact, the Prosecutor, by this exhibit, is proving the unreliability of his own evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder, then, why Madam Residovic in the motions that she filed on 28th May, 1996, when she denies so emphatically that this accused had anything to do with the INDA-BAU premises in Vienna, she would say the following: "Carrying out the Prosecutor's orders, the authorities of the Federal Republic of Germany and the Republic of Austria seized Zejnil Delalic's flats and business premises in Munich and Vienna. On this occasion they seized a large quantity of evidence which belonged to Mr. Delalic and to third persons entirely unconnected with the matter under investigation. More than 80 videotapes were seized, most of them the property of BiH society in Vienna, as well as business documents and archives of business firms co-owned or managed by Mr. Zejnil Delalic. The personal files of the employees of these firms and other documents ..." Is she suggesting now to this Chamber that she had no instructions to write this and put this in her motion? In my submission she cannot speak in forked tongue on this matter. They are either the premises of the accused in Vienna or they are not. If she said so earlier then in my submission she is estopped from now arguing that they are not his premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have the motion of the Defence and it clearly applies to various premises in Munich and Vienna, for example the company Nike, which was searched and where nothing was found, as testified by Austrian offices, is co-owned by my client. However, the firm INDA-BAU as shown by all the witnesses and there are also documents to show when INDA-BAU was founded and who were the owners and so on. I think those documents speak much more than any Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, now addressing the question of the document of 11th July, which, as I said, I should refer to it by its exhibit number, 118, is already admitted into evidence as part of Exhibit 99. I make particular reference to page 41 of the record of interview where this document is discussed, and the discussion proceeds as follows. This is the interview with Mr. Delalic on 23rd August 1996 at Scheveningen. It is said, "why is it that you kept copies of the 11th July document, but did not have any copies of the 27th July document?" In my submission, the reference to the 11th July document is a reference to Exhibit 118. The answer is, from the accused, "I had both." The investigator then says, "you had a copy of the 27th July document in Vienna or Munich" -- I emphasise Vienna -- "I have no idea, I could have been both in Vienna or in Munich." Then it goes on then to, "what authority, if any, did you have over Konjic?" In my submission the accused is not saying there, "Vienna? I know nothing about Vienna, I have never had any business premises in Vienna". He does not say that. He says, "I have no idea, I could have been both in Vienna or in Munich".

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in view of this argument there is no doubt that my client until 25th November had residents also in Vienna. Therefore, on that occasion he did not exclude the possibility that that document shown to him may have been in Vienna, but it was not this document that was shown to him, but another document which has an indication of the fax number and dated 23rd July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In any event your Honours, I do not think it is necessary to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I want to find out, does it contain the fax number and the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might have a look. Could we look at Exhibit 99?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of some help, Exhibit 99 annex 9 is the one that has the fax number across the top of it that says "INDA-BAU". I do not believe there is any fax notation at all on the other order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit 99 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask Delalic's statement to be looked at, as we are having this discussion about the facts. It was only this document that was shown to Zejnil Delalic during the interrogation, the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Were the fax machines working at the relevant time between Sarajevo and Konjic? How could there be a fax number on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly the proof, how communications functioned in -- it somehow reached Zagreb and then from Zagreb it was sent elsewhere. Sometimes it took several months for a document to reach its destination. If I may, as an amicus curiae, tell you in the middle of 1993 the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina made an analysis in which it said the official gazettes printed in Sarajevo were delayed 30 to 93 days. We had nothing there at the time. The witnesses have tried to explain to you, and the route that document took is best illustrated by the fact that apparently this document was found in Munich, at least that is what the Prosecutor says. My client said it was his document, and explained why it carried a fax number, but he did not know where it came from, and that is not this document that is now being tendered within the framework of the folder from Vienna. That is not the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was thinking about this last night. I looked at a fax from my office I forget regularly whether the fax notation is where it comes from or going to. It is where it came from. I think if we look at that telephone number it does say INDA-BAU. I do not know what the country codes are for Austria and Germany, but somebody can probably figure out where that thing came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am just wondering, Mr. Niemann, I am just wondering, you have -- you are tendering this order appointing Delalic as the Commander of the Tactical Group 1. The document which you are actually placing in the court, does it bear the fax number? Some copies may not have that number. I am just wondering.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It seems there are some that may and some that do not. May I see Exhibit 118, and I will be able to let your Honour know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are still arguing 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just want some information, that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I could see the document. There is no fax number appearing on this one, your Honours, which appears to be a copy of the document, and I hand it to your Honours to examine. Your Honours, the document that I first hand you is the one shown in the course of the record of interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which was the copy shown to Mr. Delalic when he was interviewed by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is the one I now show you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Apparently the copy which has been filed before the Tribunal does not contain this endorsement related to fax, because this is dated 23rd July, 1992, this fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is the copy that was found at the premises, your Honour. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Okay. You are producing the document which was found in the premises. Please take this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that be handed back? So it seems, your Honour, that there may well have been two copies, but in my submission that is a copy of the very same document, one being a document found in the premises, and one being a copy. From where it comes, I am not sure that I know. It may well come from Munich.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does it assume some relevancy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it seems there may have been two copies of it, one which was found at the premises in INDA-BAU in Vienna and there may well be a copy sent from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They are not both originals, copies of the fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Both copies, yes, your Honour. I submit that they are the same document, it is merely a copy. But I tender the copy found in the premises, which is number 180.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course we object, because this shows best how documents were confused and nobody ever managed to establish what was found in which folder. We simply do not know where this document comes from. The document shown to my client was one that he recognised, but witness Moerbauer showed that his markings had disappeared, which is further -- also the fact that there is no marking on this document speaks to the unreliability of all the documents coming from Vienna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next document is -- that I go to is 119. Your Honours, this is in the nature of a hand-written note, which was referred to in evidence by Officer Moerbauer at page 3652, line 16 to 18 of the transcript. He says in relation to this document: "This document was in binder I4 and was also amongst the items that were handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, following search of Koppstrasse 14. These were handed to me at the Vienna police headquarters." Your Honours, this document in the fourth numbered paragraph, it is a hand-written document, makes reference there to, "Pavo Mucic (BiH Territorial Defence) is in charge of transport". It is signed under the heading "Commander", and there is hand-written then the name, "Zejnil Delalic". There is a reference in the left-hand side of the page to the 8th May 1992, and on the hand-written copy the initials for the city of Zagreb appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is interesting. He was admitting he was in Konjic in May 1992; the place mentioned is Zagreb. That I believe is in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is indeed in Croatia, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is a date when he was not even a co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is an interesting matter your Honours. If I can take your Honour to Exhibit 124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We are talking about reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can I take you to 124?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us have a short break and come back at 4.30. (4.00 pm) (Short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Before Mr. Niemann begins, I want to formally for the record announce that we are withdrawing the request for hearing that we had filed some time within the last 10 days regarding the memorandum that was circulated to the court by the Office of the Registrar. I wanted to make it real clear now before the Prosecutor goes to the expense of flying Witness J back into The Hague and also to avoid getting into what may be a serious hurrah that Judge Jan identified about immunity of UN witnesses, and that would have something to do with they are immune when they are asked to assist the Defence but not immune when asked to assist the Prosecutor. Rather than get into all that we would withdraw and obviate the necessity of that hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Niemann has asked me to respond to this, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution would still be planning on calling Witness J because as indicated in our motion we think it is relevant evidence with respect to the issue about immunity. I think if the security guard declined to testify and we tried to subpoena him those issues would have arisen, but the security officer, excuse me, security officer has agreed to testify and has not requested any kind of privilege. Since there cannot be any doubt that a member of the United Nations is permitted to testify, there is no issue, so although we thank the Defence counsel for trying to move things along, it is still our intention to call Witness J and the security officer as evidence in the case in chief as well as potential consideration for your Honours as a separate contempt. But we are bringing it in the case as evidence in the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I apparently mistakenly relied upon Mr. Niemann's response to Judge Jan this morning. When Judge Jan inquired, Mr. Niemann said the only reason this was coming up was because we filed that motion. I thought by withdrawing that motion it would not be coming up. Apparently that was not the case. We then will have to get into some fairly serious discussions about this immunity issue, because those in charge of UN employees can very easily instruct them when they should refuse and not refuse to testify and protect them with immunity. That is extremely unfair, an egregious denial of equality of arms and perhaps something that could cause this whole case to be overturned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I am not in possession of all the facts at this moment. I have seen only one of them, the motion, which is Ms. McMurrey on behalf of Landzo. I think that is all I can talk about. In any event if your application to withdraw still stands, then no one can take notice of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it still stands. And let me just expand very briefly. The court will recall that a number of the witnesses who came here and testified about experiences in Celebici when confronted with statements which were contrary to their testimony testified that the interpreter must have made a mistake and that is not what they said. The interpreters are all UN employees and we had understood from a previous attempt to get an interpreter to testify that there was an immunity which could only be waived by the Secretary General of the United Nations. I do not know if that is the case or not, whether we were misinformed at that time or not. But if it is now the case that UN employees are not immune and may testify, then under the principle of equality of arms again we absolutely are entitled to call of those interpreters to impeach those witnesses and say their interpretations were correct and I think that is what they will say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a convention in force which relates to diplomatic personnel which also applies to UN personnel. In the case of the UN, as I understand it, Mr. Koffi-Anan, the Secretary General, has to circulate a list of those entitled to the privileges under that convention. I formally call upon the Registry to identify those persons who are interpreters as to whether or not they are on that list, or whether they have ever been on the list circulated by the Secretary General and whether there are any security guards on the list of those being entitled to the privileges of the relevant convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I want to refer to what Mr. Ackerman has said. The only case I remember here was one of the interpreter, and I do not think we relied on the UN convention for it. We thought it was mainly one of policy, public policy and the circumstances in which it all happened. Well, I suppose it depends on the nature of the issue whether such might be a valid excuse for not testifying. It is not an absolute one, because I think there are very few things which might weigh against the interest of justice. So it depends on the issue. But if your motion has any relationship with what has come in and I suppose by the Prosecutor, then it depends what that position is at the time it is being discussed, because if that has been withdrawn then perhaps you might discuss it with the Prosecutor and see what the position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
